messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For James, the moment that changed everything began with a cough. His twelve-year-old daughter, Leilani, had been tired for weeks, but he had told himself it was just the school year wearing her down. Then came the breathlessness—a frightening afternoon when she struggled to catch her breath after climbing the stairs. In the emergency room, James stood by as doctors ran tests, their faces growing increasingly serious. When they finally told him it was leukemia, the word landed like a physical blow. What haunted him most, what he replayed every single night, was the look in Leilani’s eyes as they wheeled her away for her first procedure. She had been so scared, and James had been certain that if he had just taken her to the doctor sooner, if he had pushed harder when she first complained of being tired, none of this would have happened. He had failed to protect her. He had acted too slowly, and now his daughter was fighting for her life.

In the months that followed, James became a ghost in his own life. He was still a project manager, still showed up to work each day, but the job that once gave him structure now felt like a trap. Every delay in a project timeline sent a spike of terror through his chest—if something took longer than expected, his mind immediately jumped to the worst possible conclusion. A late email from a subcontractor meant they had been in an accident. A postponed meeting meant someone had died. He could not trust his own judgment anymore. The self-doubt had crept in during those long nights in the hospital, when he second-guessed every decision he had made as a father. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally unreliable, that he could not trust himself to do the right thing, because he had already failed once in the most important role of his life.

The physical reactions were the hardest to control. A sudden shortness of breath, even from walking too fast, would send him spiraling. His chest would tighten, his heart would race, and he would be back in that hospital room, watching Leilani struggle for air. He learned to avoid anything that might trigger that feeling. He stopped going to the gym. He took the elevator instead of the stairs. He began to dread the annual physical examination his company required, knowing that lying on an exam table would bring back the helplessness of watching doctors work on his daughter. Hospitals became places of pure terror. He would cross the street to avoid walking past one, and when his wife—before she passed—needed a routine procedure, he could not bring himself to sit with her in the waiting room. He made excuses. He was busy at work. He was feeling unwell. The shame of that avoidance sat heavy in his chest, but the alternative felt worse.

To keep the memories at bay, James kept his mind occupied constantly. He listened to podcasts during every commute, worked late into the evening, and filled his weekends with home improvement projects that required his full attention. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the memories down whenever they surfaced. But the suppression took its toll. His relationships with his surviving children grew distant; they complained that he was never fully present, that his mind was always somewhere else. He had become a man who was always busy but never really there.

Now, at sixty-five, recently widowed and retired from his project management role, James has run out of distractions. The silence of his house is unbearable. The memories press in from all sides. He came to therapy because his daughter—the one who survived, now grown with children of her own—told him she was worried about him. What frightens James most is the possibility that he is right about himself: that he is a man who cannot be trusted, who failed his child, and who will never be able to make peace with what happened. He hopes, quietly and without much conviction, that someone might show him a different way to carry this weight.
